chief_complaint: progressive painful restriction of shoulder movement across all directions, difficulty dressing, and normal shoulder X-ray (Adhesive Capsulitis / Frozen Shoulder)
hpi_details: 52F with poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes presents with 6-month history of deep, aching pain and progressive severe stiffness in her left shoulder. Initially started as night pain that woke her up when sleeping on her left side ('freezing stage'). Over the past 3 months, the pain has lessened slightly, but she has lost the ability to reach behind her back to fasten her bra, reach up to grab overhead dishes, or comb her hair ('frozen stage'). Shoulder feels completely locked when attempting daily tasks.
ideas: frustrated by inability to dress herself independently or sleep through the night
concerns: worried she tore a rotator cuff tendon or has severe arthritis requiring joint replacement surgery
expectations: wants physical therapy, pain injections, and restoration of her shoulder reach

clinical_knowledge.topic: Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) evaluation and management
core_concepts: Prompt recognition and structured assessment of Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) is essential for guiding targeted diagnostic workup and clinical decision-making.
A thorough clinical history, baseline risk assessment, and targeted objective testing must be synthesized rather than relying on any single symptom in isolation.

Standard management emphasizes structured physical therapy with gentle progressive stretching and, when needed, intra-articular corticosteroid injection to reduce inflammation, adapted to individual patient risk factors and clinical severity.
Diagnostic workup and therapeutic decisions should adhere to established clinical guidelines while accounting for patient-specific comorbidities.
diagnostic_clues: Chief Complaint: progressive painful restriction of shoulder movement across all directions, difficulty dressing, and normal shoulder X-ray (Adhesive Capsulitis / Frozen Shoulder)

Key HPI features: 52F with poorly controlled Type 2 Diabetes presents with 6-month history of deep, aching pain and progressive severe stiffness in her left shoulder. Initially started as night pain that woke her up when sleeping on her left side ('freezing stage'). Over the past 3 months, the pain has lessened slightly, but she has lost the ability to reach behind her back to fasten her bra, reach up to grab overhead dishes, or comb her hair ('frozen stage'). Shoulder feels completely locked when attempting daily tasks.

Objective/Exam findings: Vitals: HR 74, BP 132/80. Shoulder exam demonstrates profound, global restriction of BOTH active and passive glenohumeral range of motion. Most severe characteristic deficits noted: passive External Rotation with arm at side is restricted to only 15 degrees (compared to 70 degrees on normal right arm); passive Abduction limited to 60 degrees; Internal Rotation limited to reaching only the sacrum/L5 level (compared to T7 on right). Rotator cuff strength testing (empty can, belly press) is normal in available range without drop-arm sign. Left shoulder X-ray (AP, true glenohumeral, and axillary views) is completely normal without glenohumeral osteoarthritis or calcific tendinitis.
Relevant background/PMH: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (HbA1c 8.4%), Hypothyroidism
Current medications: Metformin 1000mg BID, Levothyroxine 75mcg daily
common_misconceptions: Assuming that an atypical or mild presentation rules out Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder).
Relying solely on a single normal laboratory value or imaging result to prematurely exclude pathology.
Equating temporary symptomatic relief with full resolution of the underlying condition without completing standard evaluation.
Misattributing symptoms exclusively to Rotator cuff tear without completing a comprehensive diagnostic workup.
dangerous_errors: Failing to recognize red-flag features and delaying urgent escalation or emergency intervention.
Prematurely discharging or reassuring the patient before completing appropriate diagnostic assessment.
Initiating empirical treatment without considering major patient contraindications or drug interactions.
Ignoring critical warning signs such as: Night pain interfering with sleep.
management_principles: Rehabilitation therapy: initiate structured, gentle, progressive physical therapy focusing on low-load, long-duration passive and active-assisted stretching (capsular stretching, pendulum exercises, external rotation stretching using a cane or towel)
CRITICAL RULE: Avoid aggressive, painful forced stretching during the early freezing stage which exacerbates capsular inflammation

Interventional pain management: perform ultrasound- or fluoroscopy-guided Glenohumeral Joint Intra-articular Corticosteroid Injection (Triamcinolone acetonide 40 mg + Lidocaine) to reduce synovitis/capsular inflammation and facilitate physical therapy compliance
boundaries_and_exceptions: Specific drug dosages, monitoring protocols, and referral criteria must be tailored to organ function, comorbidities, and local hospital pathways.
Atypical presentations in elderly, pediatric, or immunocompromised patients may require lower thresholds for inpatient monitoring and specialist consultation.

reference_soap.subjective:
Chief Complaint: progressive painful restriction of shoulder movement across all directions, difficulty dressing, and normal shoulder X-ray (Adhesive Capsulitis / Frozen Shoulder)

Initially started as night pain that woke her up when sleeping on her left side ('freezing stage'). Over the past 3 months, the pain has lessened slightly, but she has lost the ability to reach behind her back to fasten her bra, reach up to grab overhead dishes, or comb her hair ('frozen stage'). reference_soap.objective: Vitals: HR 74, BP 132/80. Shoulder exam demonstrates profound, global restriction of BOTH active and passive glenohumeral range of motion. Most severe characteristic deficits noted: passive External Rotation with arm at side is restricted to only 15 degrees (compared to 70 degrees on normal right arm); passive Abduction limited to 60 degrees; Internal Rotation limited to reaching only the sacrum/L5 level (compared to T7 on right). Rotator cuff strength testing (empty can, belly press) is normal in available range without drop-arm sign. Left shoulder X-ray (AP, true glenohumeral, and axillary views) is completely normal without glenohumeral osteoarthritis or calcific tendinitis.
reference_soap.assessment: Idiopathic Adhesive Capsulitis (Frozen Shoulder) of the Left Glenohumeral Joint, Stage II (`Frozen` stage), strongly associated with Type 2 Diabetes.
reference_soap.plan: 1. Offer structured, gentle, progressive physical therapy emphasizing low-load, long-duration passive and active-assisted stretching; avoid aggressive, painful forced stretching. 2. If pain limits rehabilitation after clinical confirmation and contraindication review, an appropriately trained clinician may discuss image-guided glenohumeral corticosteroid injection, including the potential for transient hyperglycemia in diabetes. 3. Explain the usual prolonged course and consider hydrodilatation or surgical options only after an adequate nonoperative trial and specialist assessment.

learning_objectives: Differentiate Adhesive Capsulitis (profound loss of BOTH active AND passive range of motion, particularly external rotation, with normal X-ray) from Rotator Cuff Tear (loss of active motion with PRESERVED passive range of motion, positive drop arm/impingement tests) and Glenohumeral Osteoarthritis (loss of motion with X-ray showing joint space narrowing and osteophytes)
Identify strong epidemiological associations between Adhesive Capsulitis and endocrine disorders (Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus and Hypothyroidism carry 3-5x increased incidence)

Understand the three distinct clinical stages of frozen shoulder: Freezing (painful synovitis lasting 2-9 months), Frozen (stiffness dominating over pain lasting 4-12 months), and Thawing (gradual spontaneous resolution lasting 5-24 months)
Outline evidence-based PM&R management: intra-articular corticosteroid injection during the freezing stage combined with gentle, non-provocative physical therapy stretching regimens

teaching.one_liner: Progressive restriction of both active and passive shoulder movement due to capsular fibrosis.

must_ask.objective: Active and passive range of motion
must_ask.say: Can you lift your arm yourself, or does it feel stiff even when someone tries to raise it for you?
Is it difficult to reach behind your back or comb your hair?
Does the shoulder pain wake you up at night when you lie on that side?
Do you have diabetes or thyroid conditions?
Did the pain start gradually before the stiffness set in?
